statement: If f and g are differentiable functions at x and g(x) \neq 0, the derivative of their quotient h(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} is given by h'(x) = \frac{f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x)}{[g(x)]^2}.

symbols.meaning: increment approaching zero in the difference quotient
derivative of h with respect to x
derivative of f with respect to x
derivative of g with respect to x

steps.text: Apply the definition of the derivative to h(x): h'(x) = \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{h(x+k) - h(x)}{k}
Substitute h(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} into the difference quotient: h'(x) = \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{\frac{f(x+k)}{g(x+k)} - \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}}{k}
Find a common denominator in the numerator: h'(x) = \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{f(x+k)g(x) - f(x)g(x+k)}{k \cdot g(x)g(x+k)}
Factor the expression into a product of limits: h'(x) = \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{f(x+k)g(x) - f(x)g(x+k)}{k} \cdot \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{1}{g(x)g(x+k)}

Add and subtract f(x)g(x) in the numerator, and evaluate the second limit using continuity of g (implied by differentiability): h'(x) = \lim_{k \to 0} \left[ \frac{f(x+k)g(x) - f(x)g(x) + f(x)g(x) - f(x)g(x+k)}{k} \right] \cdot \frac{1}{[g(x)]^2}

Split the numerator into two terms and separate the limits: h'(x) = \left[ \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{f(x+k)g(x) - f(x)g(x)}{k} - \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{f(x)g(x+k) - f(x)g(x)}{k} \right] \cdot \frac{1}{[g(x)]^2}

Factor g(x) out of the first limit and f(x) out of the second limit: h'(x) = \left[ \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{f(x+k) - f(x)}{k} \cdot g(x) - f(x) \cdot \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{g(x+k) - g(x)}{k} \right] \cdot \frac{1}{[g(x)]^2}
Evaluate the limits using the definitions f'(x) = \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{f(x+k) - f(x)}{k} and g'(x) = \lim_{k \to 0} \frac{g(x+k) - g(x)}{k}: h'(x) = \frac{f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x)}{[g(x)]^2}

assumptions.assumption: f and g are differentiable at x
assumptions.breaks_when: f'(x) or g'(x) does not exist

failure_modes.cause: f or g is not differentiable at x
